p167.lead: From Philadelphia to Bethany: the lowest seat and the parable of the great supper, the woman loosed from a spirit of infirmity, word of Lazarus, the Pharisee and the publican, marriage and children, and the angels.

p167.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p167.s0.h: Introduction — Proclaimed with Power, Without Miracles
p167.s0.b0: During the Perean ministry Jesus was usually accompanied by ten apostles, since at least two always stayed at Pella to teach the crowds there. This time Peter and Andrew went back to Pella, and when Jesus arrived at Philadelphia he had more than six hundred followers with him.
p167.s0.b1: The text stresses again that, apart from the ten lepers, there were no miracles on this mission. The gospel was proclaimed with power without miracles, and for the most part without the personal presence of Jesus or his apostles. Arriving at Philadelphia on February 22, the company rested for two days and heard good news from Alexandria and Damascus.
p167.s1.h: I. Breakfast with the Pharisees — The Lowest Seat and the Guest Who Cannot Repay
p167.s1.b0: A wealthy Pharisee of Philadelphia who had accepted Abner’s teaching gave a Sabbath breakfast in Jesus’ honor, to which some forty leading citizens and lawyers were invited. A Pharisee from Jerusalem, a former member of the Sanhedrin, made for the seat of honor as was his habit, was moved four places down, and was deeply offended.
p167.s1.b1: Near the end of the meal a believer suffering from severe dropsy came in. He did not ask to be healed, but he hoped to gain the Master’s compassion here, away from the crowds. Jesus smiled kindly at him and asked the guests whether it was lawful to heal the sick on the Sabbath. No one answered.

p167.s1.b2.q: You have not asked to be healed, but I know the desire of your heart and the faith of your soul.

p167.s1.b3: Jesus said that the Father does such works not to tempt people into the kingdom but to reveal himself to those already in it. Then, apparently with the scramble for the seat of honor in mind, he told them not to seek the chief seats at a feast, and urged them to invite those who cannot repay.

head: Lesson of the feast
The world’s habit
Jesus’ counsel
rows: Where to sit
Take the chief seat first
Take the lowest place — raising you up is the host’s part
Whom to invite
Friends, kinsmen, and rich neighbors who will return the favor
The poor, the maimed, and the blind, who cannot repay
The reward
Hospitality returned in kind
A blessing in one’s own heart

p167.s1.b5.q: Forget not, every one who exalts himself shall be humbled, while he who truly humbles himself shall be exalted.

p167.s2.h: II. Parable of the Great Supper — A Meaning Each Must Find in His Own Soul
p167.s2.b0: To break the awkward silence, a lawyer offered the common saying that blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God, and Jesus answered with the parable of the great supper. Those invited excused themselves on account of a field, oxen, and a marriage, so the master sent for the poor and outcast from the streets and lanes, and even for people from the highways and hedges, until his house was full.

head: Who was invited
The excuse
rows: The first man
He had just bought a farm and had to go and see it
The second man
He had bought five yoke of oxen and had to go and receive them
The third man
He had just married a wife and could not come
Those who came in at last
The poor and outcast of the streets, and people from the highways and hedges

p167.s2.b2: At least one of the Pharisees who sneered that day grasped the meaning of the parable, was baptized, and publicly confessed his faith. The next day the apostles each tried to interpret the parable, but Jesus only listened with interest and offered no further explanation.

p167.s2.b3.q: Let every man find out the meaning for himself and in his own soul.

p167.s3.h: III. The Woman with the Spirit of Infirmity — Loosed from the Bondage of Fear
p167.s3.b0: On that Sabbath Jesus taught in a synagogue for the first time since the synagogues had been closed to him by order of the Sanhedrin. After the service he went over to an elderly woman who for more than eighteen years had been bowed down by fear and had lost all joy in life, and he laid his hand on her shoulder. She believed his words and by faith straightened up at once.

p167.s3.b1.q: Woman, if you would only believe, you could be wholly loosed from your spirit of infirmity.

p167.s3.b2: The text makes clear that this woman’s affliction was entirely mental and that her bent body was the result of her depressed mind. The people thought a physical disease had been cured, and the hostile ruler of the synagogue was indignant at a Sabbath healing. Jesus answered that they would loose an ox on the Sabbath to lead it to water, so should not this daughter of Abraham be loosed from bondage to drink the waters of life? That ruler was later removed from office.
p167.s3.b3: Jesus often freed victims of fear in this way from the spirit of infirmity and depression of mind. People regarded all such afflictions as bodily disease or possession by evil spirits, but the text shows plainly how deeply the state of the mind affects the body. To be released from fear can itself be healing.
p167.s4.h: IV. The Message from Bethany — One Last Appeal
p167.s4.b0: Late on the night of February 26, word came from Martha and Mary that the one the Master loved was very sick. After a strange interval in which he seemed to commune with something beyond himself, Jesus said that this sickness was not unto death and would serve to glorify God.
p167.s4.b1: His first human thought was to go at once to help them. But another idea came into his combined mind: to make this final appeal, giving the Jerusalem leaders one more chance, the most profound outward ministry of his earth life, if the Father would allow it. He had refused any display of political power, but he sought the Father’s consent to show his power over life and death.
p167.s4.b2: The Jews of the time believed that the soul might linger near the body for three days but departed after the third, and that no one had ever come back from the grave after the fourth day. For this reason Jesus stayed two full days longer at Philadelphia. Then on Wednesday morning he said, “Let us go into Judea.”

p167.s4.b3.q: As long as my day lasts, I fear not to enter Judea.

p167.s4.b4: The apostles conferred under James’s leadership and were united in opposing the journey. Jesus said that while his day lasted he was not afraid, and that he would go to wake Lazarus from sleep. When they did not understand, he told them plainly that Lazarus was dead. Then Thomas spoke up before his fellows with his resolve.

p167.s4.b5.q: if that is the Master’s choice, then let us acquit ourselves like men of courage; let us go also that we may die with him.

p167.s4.b6: The text says that in matters requiring deliberate and sustained courage, Thomas was always the mainstay of the twelve. Here we see another side of a man too easily remembered only as the doubter.
p167.s5.h: V. On the Way to Bethany — The Pharisee and the Publican, and Marriage
p167.s5.b0: At noon Jesus taught on “The Conditions of Salvation,” saying that salvation is the free gift of God to all who have faith. God’s favor cannot be bought with self-righteous works. He then told the parable of the Pharisee and the publican who prayed in the temple; it was the publican who went home justified before God.

head: Contrast
The Pharisee
The publican
rows: Standard of judgment
Judged himself by the lowest standard
Squared himself by the highest ideal
Use of devotion
A means to self-righteous inactivity and false spiritual security
A means of stirring the soul to repentance, confession, and forgiveness
What he sought
Justice
Mercy

p167.s5.b2.q: The law of the universe is: Ask and you shall receive; seek and you shall find.

p167.s5.b3: That night in Jericho the Pharisees tried to trap him over divorce. Jesus would not be drawn into a dispute over divorce laws, yet he exalted marriage as the most ideal and highest of all human relationships. He sharply condemned the practice of putting away wives for trivial reasons and pointed out the injustice it did to women and children. He endorsed only teachings that granted women equality with men.
p167.s5.b4: The apostles could not understand why he avoided definite statements on scientific, social, economic, and political questions. It was because his mission was devoted to the revelation of spiritual and religious truth. That night he explained that his carrying out his mission alone was no reflection on the desirability of marriage.

p167.s5.b5.q: in the creation of whom these parents become copartners with the Makers of heaven and earth.

p167.s6.h: VI–VII. Blessing the Little Children; The Talk about Angels
p167.s6.b0: The next morning mothers crowded in with their children, and when the apostles rebuked them, Jesus was indignant and told them not to forbid the children to come. He laid his hands on the children and gave the mothers courage and hope. The text notes that the intelligences of Nebadon were watching as these children played with the Creator of a universe.
p167.s6.b1: The text then says that the status of women in Palestine was greatly improved by Jesus’ teaching, and adds that the same would have been true throughout the world had his followers not departed so far from what he taught. His regard for marriage and for children reached well beyond the customs of his time.
p167.s6.b2: At Jericho Jesus stressed the great value of beauty in awakening the urge to worship in the early religious training of children. A child should first meet worship in nature, and afterward go to places of public worship marked by simplicity and beauty.

p167.s6.b3.q: Beauty is most religious when it is most simple and naturelike.

p167.s6.b4: On the road up to Bethany, Nathaniel asked what they should teach about angels. Jesus’ answer sums up the nature and ministry of angels concisely. The talk was cut short when Martha came hurrying out to meet him.

head: About angels
Jesus’ teaching
rows: Origin
A separate order of created beings, directly created; they do not reproduce
Relation to man
Spirit kin only; mortal man never becomes an angel
Nature
Undying but neither all-knowing nor all-powerful; the loyal angels are pure and holy
What they do not do
They are not spies reporting human thoughts to the Father — the Father’s spirit already lives within man
What they do
Carry tidings between worlds, help in the work of saving men, and escort the soul to the mansion worlds after death

p167.s6.b6.q: Angels are the sure and heavenly guides of the soul of man during that uncharted and indefinite period of time which intervenes between the death of the flesh and the new life in the spirit abodes.

p167.s7.b0: Paper 167 records the journey just before the great event of the raising of Lazarus, yet the teachings along the way all point to everyday life: where to sit at a feast, whom to invite, how to pray, how to treat marriage and children. Even with a great work ahead of him, Jesus did not neglect small people and small places.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Take the lower seat rather than seek the chief place
Whoever humbles himself shall be exalted (167:1.5)
Invite to my table those who cannot repay
Bid the poor (167:1.5)
Do not put off the invitation because I am busy
The parable of the great supper (167:2.2)
Help lift by faith those weighed down by fear and depression
The woman loosed from her infirmity (167:3.1)
Measure myself against the highest ideal, not against others
The Pharisee and the publican (167:5.2)
Open a child’s way to worship through nature and beauty
Beauty is most religious when most simple (167:6.6)

p167.s7.b2: In the next paper, Paper 168, “The Resurrection of Lazarus,” Jesus stands before the tomb at Bethany.
p168.lead: “I am the resurrection and the life”: tears before the tomb at Bethany, a unique resurrection in the form of the flesh, the Sanhedrin’s decision, and ten teachings on the answer to prayer.

p168.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p168.s0.h: Introduction — A Master Who Seemed to Come Too Late
p168.s0.b0: It was a little after noon on Thursday when Jesus came over the hill near Bethany. Lazarus had been dead four days; he had been laid in the family tomb at the end of the garden on Sunday afternoon, and that morning the stone had been rolled across the entrance. The sisters believed that if the Master had only spoken a word of healing, Lazarus would have been made whole, so they thought he had received the news too late.
p168.s0.b1: What puzzled them still more was the word brought back by the messenger on Tuesday: this sickness was not unto death. Mary, overwhelmed with grief, gave up hope, but Martha clung to hope until the moment the stone was rolled into place and posted a neighbor boy to watch the Jericho road.
p168.s0.b2: When Martha met Jesus she fell at his feet and said that had he been there her brother would not have died, yet she voiced no doubt or criticism. She said she believed in the resurrection at the last day, and Jesus looked straight into her eyes and answered her.

p168.s0.b3.q: I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me, though he dies, yet shall he live.

p168.s0.b4: Martha confessed that she had long believed him to be the Son of the living God. She called Mary secretly, hoping to avoid the many enemies from Jerusalem who were present, but that plan failed when all who had come to console Mary followed her out.
p168.s0.b5: When Mary too fell at his feet with the same words, Jesus’ soul was moved with compassion. But his human mind was deeply troubled, torn between love for the bereaved sisters and distaste for the outward mourning of those who harbored murderous intent. Among the mourners, of course, were also true friends of the family who grieved sincerely.
p168.s1.h: I. At the Tomb of Lazarus — Why Jesus Wept
p168.s1.b0: Jesus asked where they had laid him, and as he walked to the tomb, he wept. Friendly onlookers said, “See how he loved him,” while his enemies sneered that if he loved him, why had he come so late? The narrator honestly admits that he is not wholly certain of the real cause of Jesus’ weeping, and offers several thoughts.

head: Possible reason for his tears
The text’s explanation
rows: Sympathy for the sisters
He felt a genuine and deep human affection for Martha and Mary in the loss of their brother
Mixed feelings about the mourners
Sincere grief was mingled with pretended mourning, and he always disliked outward displays of mourning
Reluctance to call him back
Knowing the bitter persecution Lazarus would suffer because of his resurrection, he hesitated to bring his friend back to mortal life

p168.s1.b2: The text adds a striking detail. Jesus appeared to act within the limited knowledge of the human mind, yet his Personalized Adjuster had issued an order, just fifteen minutes before Lazarus died, that Lazarus’s Thought Adjuster be held on the planet indefinitely. Whether the divine mind of Jesus knew in advance, the narrator says only that he cannot tell.

p168.s1.b3.q: We do not know. We know only what we are herewith placing on record.

p168.s1.b4: When Jesus ordered the stone taken away, Mary hoped for a resurrection, but Martha hesitated, saying that after four days the body would have begun to decay. Jesus asked whether he had not said at the outset that this sickness was not unto death, and how long it would take them to believe and obey. The apostles and neighbors rolled the stone away.
p168.s1.b5: The Jews of the time firmly believed that the soul might linger near the tomb until the end of the third day but departed before the fourth day dawned. A resurrection on the fourth day was therefore, for everyone present, an unquestionably genuine case. Here we see why Jesus had stayed two more days at Philadelphia.
p168.s2.h: II. The Resurrection of Lazarus — The First and Last on Urantia
p168.s2.b0: At half past two on Thursday afternoon, about forty-five people stood before the tomb. They did not know that a vast host of celestial beings of every order, under the direction of Gabriel, waited close by for the signal. The text calls this event the greatest manifestation of divine power during Michael’s life in the flesh.
p168.s2.b1: A resurrection in the likeness of the mortal flesh involves far greater practical difficulties than the usual resurrection in morontia form, and requires far more celestial personalities and universe facilities. Jesus lifted his eyes, gave thanks to the Father, and then called Lazarus with a loud voice.

p168.s2.b2.q: because of those who stand here with me, I thus speak with you, that they may believe that you have sent me into the world, and that they may know that you are working with me in that which we are about to do.

head: Sequence
What happened
rows: 1. Prayer and summons
Jesus thanked the Father and cried, “Lazarus, come forth!”
2. The celestial host acts
They moved in unison in obedience to the Creator’s word
3. Twelve seconds
The lifeless form stirred and sat up on the edge of the stone shelf
4. The Adjuster’s return
The Personalized Adjuster ordered Lazarus’s waiting Adjuster to return to his mind and soul
5. The record
Gabriel recorded that this resurrection in the form of the flesh was the first and last on Urantia

p168.s2.b4: Apart from the apostles and the sisters, most fled home in fear. Lazarus asked why he was dressed in grave clothes and had awakened in the garden, and Martha had to explain his death and resurrection. He could tell nothing at all about the four days in the tomb.

p168.s2.b5.q: Time is nonexistent to those who sleep the sleep of death.

p168.s2.b6: Lifting up the kneeling Lazarus, Jesus told him that what had happened to him would be experienced in a more glorious form by all who believe this gospel. Then he said they should all go into the house and take nourishment for their bodies. These plain words, spoken just after the greatest display of power, show that this power is one with the love that cares for ordinary human needs.

p168.s2.b7.q: You shall be a living witness of the truth which I spoke—I am the resurrection and the life.

p168.s3.h: III. Meeting of the Sanhedrin — A Death Sentence Before Any Trial
p168.s3.b0: Many believed because of this, but others only hardened their hearts. Lazarus’s testimony strengthened the faith of believers, but it did little to change the attitude of the Jerusalem leaders; instead it hastened their decision to destroy Jesus. The same event produced opposite results according to the hearts that received it.

head: The Sanhedrin’s moves
The text’s record
rows: Friday’s meeting
A Pharisee proposed an unprecedented resolution to put Jesus to death at once, without trial
Fourteen resignations
The resolution never came to a vote; fourteen members withdrew and never returned
Five expulsions
Members thought friendly to Jesus were ousted, leaving the council nineteen short
Testimony of Lazarus and his sisters
The council virtually admitted the resurrection but ascribed the miracle to the prince of devils
The reason for their fear
That all the people would believe in him, and that messianic hopes would bring conflict with Rome

p168.s3.b2.q: It is better that one man die, than that the community perish.

p168.s3.b3: It was at this meeting that Caiaphas the high priest first voiced that old adage. Though warned, Jesus was not disturbed, and he rested over the Sabbath with friends at Bethpage. On Sunday morning he said farewell to the family at Bethany and set out on the road back to Pella.
p168.s4.h: IV. The Answer to Prayer — Ten Points
p168.s4.b0: On the way to Pella the apostles were deeply troubled that Lazarus had actually died despite the promise that his sickness was not unto death. They kept coming back to the question of prayer and its answer. Jesus declined to discuss the details of the resurrection as beyond their understanding, but he answered their questions about prayer freely. The text summarizes his answer in ten points.

head: Point
What it says
rows: 1. The finite and the infinite
Prayer is the finite mind’s effort to approach the Infinite, so its answer is conditioned by the purposes of the Infinite
2. Delay
An apparently unanswered prayer often betokens a better answer delayed — Lazarus had been dead eleven hours when the word was spoken
3. Answers in eternity
Some prayers are so vast they can be received only on Paradise
4. Recognized after survival
The answer may be recognized only after the one who prayed has advanced to the spirit level
5. Translated answers
Prayers distorted by ignorance and superstition are answered in altered form by spirit beings
6. Spiritual answers
True prayers are addressed to spiritual beings and answered in spiritual realities
7. Faith’s delegation
Faith grants in advance to those who hear prayer the right to answer it in their wisdom and love
8. Child and parent
A parent may answer a child’s request by delaying, modifying, or going beyond it
9. Answers held in trust
Answers not yet timely are held in trust until we reach the level to receive them
10. The time-space factor
Every genuine spirit-born petition is certain of an answer, but the factor of time and space must be reckoned with

p168.s4.b2.q: No sincere prayer is denied an answer except when the superior viewpoint of the spiritual world has devised a better answer

p168.s4.b3.q: Material beings can pray effectively only when they “pray in the spirit.”

p168.s4.b4: This teaching helps us understand prayer not as a device for getting wishes granted but as a relationship. It is always a child’s right to ask of a parent, and it is always within a parent’s duty to modify the answer by higher wisdom. The assurance that waiting is not refusal brings deep peace to those who pray without yet seeing an answer.

p168.s4.b5.q: All genuine spirit-born petitions are certain of an answer.

p168.s5.b0: Lazarus stayed at Bethany until the day of Jesus’ crucifixion, the object of attention from believers and the curious alike. But the Sanhedrin, judging that killing Jesus would accomplish little while Lazarus lived to testify, decreed his death as well. Already suffering bitter persecution, he fled across the Jordan to Abner at Philadelphia.
p168.s5.b1: Martha and Mary also disposed of their property at Bethany and joined him. Lazarus became treasurer of the church at Philadelphia and supported Abner in his disputes with Paul and the Jerusalem church; he died at sixty-seven of the same sickness that had taken him in his younger years. The persecution Jesus foresaw at the tomb did indeed follow him through life.
p168.s6.b0: Paper 168 records the greatest manifestation of divine power in Jesus’ life on earth, yet at its heart are a weeping Jesus, two waiting sisters, and a prayer whose answer seemed late. That even the greatest miracle could not change hardened hearts reminds us that faith depends more on an open heart than on evidence. And the teaching on prayer shows a way to keep trusting even while we wait.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: In grief, confess faith rather than resentment
Martha’s confession (168:0.7)
Weep sincerely with others in their sorrow
Jesus’ tears (168:1.3)
Say honestly “I don’t know” when you don’t
The narrator’s attitude (168:1.7)
Do not take a delayed answer for a refusal
A better answer delayed (168:4.5)
Entrust the answer to prayer to wisdom and love
Faith’s delegation (168:4.10)
Accept the factor of time and keep praying
The time-space factor (168:4.13)

p168.s6.b2: In the next paper, Paper 169, “Last Teaching at Pella,” Jesus leaves Bethany and continues his teaching at the camp at Pella.
p169.lead: The last week at Pella: the parables of the lost son and the shrewd steward, and how Jesus revealed God not as a king but as a Father.

p169.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p169.s0.h: Introduction — A Peak Week Amid Gathering Opposition
p169.s0.b0: Late on Monday evening, March 6, Jesus and the ten apostles reached the Pella camp. The week that followed was to be his last there. Every afternoon he preached to the crowds, and every night he answered questions from the apostles and the more advanced disciples. Word of the resurrection of Lazarus had arrived two days ahead of him, and the whole camp was astir; the narrator remarks that nothing since the feeding of the five thousand had so fired the imagination of the people.
p169.s0.b1: Yet at this very height of the second phase of the public ministry, the Pharisees and the chief priests were beginning to formulate their charges. Their objections fall under four heads, and the list shows which parts of Jesus’ teaching most troubled the religious leaders of his day.

head: The charge
The grounds they gave
rows: A friend of publicans and sinners
He receives the ungodly and even eats with them
A blasphemer
He speaks of God as his Father and thinks himself equal with God
A lawbreaker
He heals on the Sabbath and in many other ways flouts the law
In league with devils
He works wonders by the power of Beelzebub

p169.s0.b3: The paper records four scenes from that week: the stories of three lost things told to the multitude, the parable of the steward given in answer to the apostles, an old allegory recited by Peter in the midst of an uproar, and the narrator’s summary of the names and ways by which Jesus revealed God. What stands out is that, just as the accusations grew darker, the message Jesus pressed hardest was not judgment but the Father’s searching love.
p169.s1.h: I. Parable of the Lost Son — The Father Who Seeks First
p169.s1.b0: On Thursday afternoon Jesus preached on the “⟦Q 169:1.1⟧Grace of Salvation.⟦/Q⟧” He retold the stories of the lost sheep and the lost coin and then added his favorite, the parable of the prodigal son. He granted that the prophets had always urged men to seek God, but he added something new to their counsel.

p169.s1.b1.q: But I have come to show you that, while you are seeking to find God, God is likewise seeking to find you.

p169.s1.b2.q: The fact that souls are lost only increases the interest of the heavenly Father.

p169.s1.b3: People had been taught that divine acceptance follows repentance and comes as the fruit of sacrifice and penitence. Jesus reversed the order. The Father accepts us even before we repent, and he sends the Son and his associates to find the lost and bring them home. This declaration—that grace is not the reward for merit but the starting point—still brings deep relief to readers today.

p169.s1.b4.q: but I assure you that the Father accepts you even before you have repented

p169.s1.b5: The two sons in the parable have opposite temperaments. The younger is cheerful but shirks responsibility; the elder is hard-working but self-centered and conceited. The younger squanders his inheritance, ends up feeding swine, comes to himself, and turns for home. His father, watching for him, sees him while he is still far off and runs out to meet him, and the son never gets the chance to finish his confession.

p169.s1.b6.q: for this my son was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.

p169.s1.b7: The story then turns to the elder brother’s anger. For years, he protests, he has never transgressed a single command, and yet he was never given so much as a kid to make merry with his friends. Because the father loves both sons, he goes out to reason with the elder and reminds him that all he has is already his. The narrator explains why Jesus liked to tell the three stories together.

head: Story
How it was lost
The truth it shows
rows: The lost sheep
Strayed unintentionally from the path of life
The Father goes out, with his Sons, the true shepherds, to seek it
The lost coin
Spiritually blinded by the material cares and accumulations of life
How thorough is the divine searching
The lost son
Left the father’s house deliberately
How complete is the restoration into the Father’s house and heart

p169.s1.b9: The elder brother mirrors a trap that long and faithful service can set. He stayed at his father’s side, yet he did not share his father’s joy. Once service becomes a matter of reckoning rewards, a feast for a returning brother looks like injustice. The father does not scold him; he calls him “my son” and invites him into the rejoicing.
p169.s1.b10: Jesus told this story of the prodigal son many, many times over the years of his teaching. The narrator tells us that this parable and the story of the good Samaritan were his favorite ways of teaching the love of the Father and the neighborliness of man.
p169.s2.h: II. Parable of the Shrewd Steward — Foresight for Eternity
p169.s2.b0: One evening Simon Zelotes asked what Jesus had meant by saying that the children of the world are wiser in their generation than the children of the kingdom. Jesus reminded the apostles that some of them had been very shrewd in business before they entered the kingdom. If they had been so diligent in making gains for themselves, why should they be less diligent in gaining souls, now that they were stewards of God?
p169.s2.b1: The steward of the parable had oppressed his master’s clients and squandered his master’s funds, and he was about to be dismissed. So he reduced the bonds of his master’s debtors, making friends who would welcome him once he was put out. Even his master had to admit that he had shown sagacity in providing for the future. What Jesus commended was not the dishonesty but the farseeing diligence.

head: Debtor
Original debt
Rewritten bond
rows: The first debtor
A hundred measures of oil
Fifty
Another debtor
A hundred measures of wheat
Fourscore
Numerous other debtors
Reduced in the same way

p169.s2.b3.q: I affirm that he who is faithful in little will also be faithful in much, while he who is unrighteous in little will also be unrighteous in much.

p169.s2.b4: The parable neither praises nor condemns wealth as such. Jesus’ question is how we handle what has been entrusted to us. If we have shown no foresight and integrity in the affairs of this world, how can we be faithful when entrusted with the true riches of the heavenly kingdom? The question applies just as directly to our workplaces and households today.
p169.s2.b5: Jesus urged his hearers to live so as to make eternal friendship with the forces of righteousness, and he closed with the saying that no one can serve God and mammon. The Pharisees, much given to acquiring riches, sneered and tried to draw him into argument, but he refused to debate with his enemies and withdrew to his tent. His refusal to be drawn into unprofitable dispute is itself a lesson.
p169.s3.h: III. The Rich Man and the Beggar — An Old Parable Retold by Peter
p169.s3.b0: When the meeting grew too noisy, Simon Peter stood up and took charge. What the Master had said, he told them, was no new doctrine, and he recited the old allegory of the Nazarites that John the Baptist used to thunder at those who loved riches. Peter made it clear, however, that this parable was not according to the gospel they preached.
p169.s3.b1: In the story a rich man named Dives lives in splendor every day, while at his gate lies Lazarus, a beggar covered with sores. After death their positions are reversed, and when Dives begs that someone be sent to warn his five brothers, the request is refused.
p169.s3.b2: The allegory served as a warning against a life that enjoys wealth while failing to see the suffering at its own door. Peter said the people would do well to heed its lessons until they came to comprehend the new light of the kingdom of heaven. The story was offered, in other words, not as a substitute for the gospel but as a stepping-stone for those who had not yet reached its new light.

p169.s3.b3.q: If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded even if one were to rise from the dead.

p169.s3.b4: Jesus’ own attitude is worth noticing. The apostles and disciples often asked him about this parable, but he never consented to comment on it. The narrator sets the story apart as an ancient parable of the Nazarite brotherhood, not as Jesus’ own teaching. Readers do well to keep this distinction in mind and to take from it, with care, only its warning about riches.
p169.s4.h: IV. The Father and His Kingdom — Not a King but a Father
p169.s4.b0: The apostles proclaimed the kingdom of God, yet they could hardly grasp that the Father in heaven was not a king. People then knew of kings and emperors as rulers, and the Jews had long awaited a coming kingdom. So the Master thought it best to call the spiritual brotherhood of man the kingdom of heaven and its spirit head the Father in heaven. Never once did he refer to his Father as a king.
p169.s4.b1: Jesus gave no systematic lessons about the Father, nor did he offer arguments to prove the Father’s reality. His teaching centered on the declaration that he and the Father are one. The way to learn of God is not to analyze his words but to observe the divinity of his life.

p169.s4.b2.q: You can know God, not by understanding what Jesus said, but by knowing what Jesus was.

rows: God

p169.s4.b4: Except when quoting the Hebrew scriptures, Jesus referred to Deity by only two names: God and Father. Instead of Yahweh, which stood for the tribal God of the Jews, he used the Hebrew word signifying the plural God, and he exalted the deity of a race into the Father of all men. He taught, moreover, that the God of universes and the Father of all men are one and the same Paradise Deity.
p169.s4.b5: Jesus never claimed to be the manifestation of Elohim in the flesh. He proclaimed himself instead the revelation of the Father in the flesh. In fact, he taught only two things about God: that God in himself is spirit, and that in all his relations with his creatures he is a Father.

p169.s4.b6.q: To hear Jesus’ teaching is not equivalent to knowing God, but to see Jesus is an experience which in itself is a revelation of the Father to the soul.

p169.s4.b7: The paper likens Jesus to a spiritual lens in human likeness that makes the invisible One visible to material creatures. Yet all of this must take place in the personal experience of the individual believer, for God who is spirit can be known only as a spiritual experience.

p169.s4.b8.q: The God of universes rules the far-flung creation, but it is the Father in heaven who sends forth his spirit to dwell within your minds.

p169.s5.b0: Paper 169 begins with people seeking God and moves to the Father who seeks people first. The parable of the prodigal son teaches the order of grace; the parable of the steward teaches diligence for eternity; and the final section teaches that the way to know God lies less in doctrine than in the experience of beholding the life of Jesus.

p169.s5.b2: The next paper, Paper 170, “⟦Q 169:1.14⟧The Kingdom of Heaven⟦/Q⟧,” sets out more fully the teaching about the kingdom that Jesus gave at Pella in this period.
p170.lead: The last sermon at Pella: sorting out the many ideas of the kingdom of heaven, recasting it as the personal experience of doing God’s will, and distinguishing church from kingdom.

p170.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p170.s0.b0: On Saturday afternoon, March 11, Jesus preached his last sermon at Pella. The narrator counts it among the notable addresses of the public ministry, a full and complete discussion of the kingdom of heaven. Jesus used “⟦Q 170:0.1⟧kingdom of heaven⟦/Q⟧” and “⟦Q 170:0.1⟧kingdom of God⟦/Q⟧” interchangeably, but his hearers were confused about what the terms meant.

p170.s0.b1.q: The idea of a temporal king was too deep-rooted in the Jewish mind thus to be dislodged in a single generation.

p170.s0.b2: The problem was not the word itself but the expectations attached to it. The hope of an earthly king ran too deep in the Jewish mind to be uprooted in one generation. The narrator tells us that he will amplify this address with sayings Jesus gave on other occasions and with remarks made to the apostles that same evening, and that he will also comment on how the kingdom idea later worked itself out in the Christian church.
p170.s1.h: I. Concepts of the Kingdom of Heaven — A Tangled Inheritance
p170.s1.b0: The Hebrew scriptures already held a dual concept of the kingdom. The prophets presented it both as a present reality and as a future hope to be fulfilled with the Messiah. To these were added the later Jewish idea of a transcendental kingdom and the Persian idea of a final contest between good and evil, and just before Jesus came the Jews had blended them all into an apocalyptic expectation of an age of Jewish triumph.

rows: A present reality
The kingdom here and now, as the prophets presented it
A future hope

The later Jewish concept
A world-wide and transcendental kingdom of supernatural origin and miraculous inauguration
The Persian teaching
A divine kingdom established at the end of the world, when good triumphs over evil

head: Ideas of the kingdom in the Christian era
Character
rows: The concept of the Jews
An age of national triumph to be set up by the Messiah

The final victory of good at the end of the world

“The kingdom of heaven within you”

p170.s1.b3: In choosing the term kingdom of heaven, Jesus took up the most vital heritage of both the Jewish and Persian religions. Yet to his apostles he always taught the kingdom as a personal experience—man’s experience in relation to his fellows on earth and to the Father in heaven.

p170.s1.b4.q: Concerning the kingdom, his last word always was, “The kingdom is within you.”

p170.s1.b5: The narrator traces centuries of confusion to three causes: the successive phases through which the kingdom idea passed as Jesus and the apostles recast it, the transplanting of early Christianity from Jewish to gentile soil, and the drift by which the gospel of the kingdom became more and more a religion about Jesus.
p170.s2.h: II. Jesus’ Concept of the Kingdom — Doing the Will of God
p170.s2.b0: Jesus made it plain that the kingdom must rest on the truth of the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man. Accepting this teaching, he declared, would free man from the age-long bondage of animal fear and give him new courage and spiritual power, new comfort, a new moral standard, and spiritual attainment as the true goal of living.
p170.s2.b1: The central effort of the sermon was to translate the kingdom into the ideal of doing God’s will. In place of kingdom, king, and subjects, Jesus wanted to give the picture of a heavenly family, a heavenly Father, and liberated sons of God serving their fellows with joy. Yet the narrator records, without ornament, that he did not succeed.

p170.s2.b2.q: The great effort embodied in this sermon was the attempt to translate the concept of the kingdom of heaven into the ideal of the idea of doing the will of God.

head: Two phases of the kingdom
Content
rows: The kingdom of God in this world
The supreme desire to do the will of God; the unselfish love of man which yields the good fruits of improved ethical and moral conduct
The kingdom of God in heaven
The goal of mortal believers, where the love for God is perfected and the will of God is done more divinely

p170.s2.b4: By this time the apostles saw the kingdom in two ways: as a personal experience already present in the believer’s heart, and as a world event still to come, suddenly and spectacularly. Jesus never tired of telling them that the kingdom was their personal experience of realizing the higher qualities of spiritual living, an experience that grows to ever higher levels of certainty and grandeur. This gradual growth is what the parables of the leaven and the mustard seed point to.
p170.s2.b5: By faith the believer enters the kingdom now. Jesus named two things essential to that entrance: sincere faith, receiving sonship as a gift with the open mind of a little child, and truth hunger, the thirst for righteousness.

p170.s2.b6.q: Jesus taught that sin is not the child of a defective nature but rather the offspring of a knowing mind dominated by an unsubmissive will.

p170.s2.b7: He taught that God has already forgiven, and that when we forgive our fellows we create in our own souls the capacity to receive that forgiveness. Jesus tried many substitutes for the word kingdom—the kingdom of life, the family of God, the Father’s will, the brotherhood of man, and others—but in the end he could not escape the kingdom idea.
p170.s3.h: III. In Relation to Righteousness — Religion the Cause, Ethics the Result
p170.s3.b0: Jesus taught that by faith we must acquire a righteousness exceeding the righteousness of slavish works that some scribes and Pharisees paraded before the world. Childlike faith is the key that opens the door of the kingdom, but once inside there are progressive steps of righteousness to climb in order to grow to the full stature of the sons of God.

head: Step of inner righteousness
Content
rows: God’s forgiveness is personally experienced just in so far as a man forgives his fellows
A man will not truly forgive his fellows unless he loves them as himself
To love your neighbor as yourself is the highest ethics
Moral conduct, true righteousness, becomes the natural result of such love

p170.s3.b2.q: But Jesus did not put ethics in the place of religion. He taught religion as a cause and ethics as a result.

p170.s3.b3.q: The righteousness of any act must be measured by the motive; the highest forms of good are therefore unconscious.

p170.s3.b4: Because every act is to be judged by its motive, the highest good is done unconsciously. The religion of the kingdom is personal, but its fruits are familial and social. The deeper our inward fellowship with God, the more naturally it overflows into loving service, so this section offers a practical counsel: never separate faith from its practice.
p170.s4.h: IV. Jesus’ Teaching about the Kingdom — Five Phases and Five Features
p170.s4.b0: Jesus never gave a precise definition of the kingdom. In this sermon he pointed instead to five phases, or epochs, of it. For that reason, the narrator says, whenever Jesus uses the word kingdom we must ask which phase he has in mind.

head: Five phases of the kingdom
Five cardinal features of the gospel
rows: The inward experience of the individual believer’s fellowship with the Father
The pre-eminence of the individual
The enlarging brotherhood of believers — the social aspects of enhanced morals and quickened ethics
The will as the determining factor in man’s experience
The supermortal brotherhood of invisible spiritual beings
Spiritual fellowship with God the Father
The dawn of a new social order — the next age of man
The supreme satisfactions of the loving service of man
The kingdom in its fullness — the age of light and life
The transcendency of the spiritual over the material in human personality

p170.s4.b2.q: Neither make the fatal mistake, in looking for the age manifestation of the kingdom, of failing to effect its establishment within your own souls.

p170.s4.b3: The narrator urges us not to be discouraged if the kingdom seems slow in coming. Progressive evolution, material and spiritual alike, is subject to sudden periodical changes, and Jesus’ bestowal was itself just such an unexpected event. Meanwhile Michael and his associates, by gradually changing the wills of men, are slowly but surely changing the whole course of human evolution.
p170.s4.b4: Jesus promised a future revelation of the kingdom, and he promised to return in person, but he never said that the two were the same event. The apostles and disciples hastily linked them and lived in hope of an immediate second coming. The narrator keeps a careful reserve: these promises may, or may not, refer to the same event.
p170.s5.h: V. Later Ideas of the Kingdom — Church and Kingdom
p170.s5.b0: The narrator then describes how the kingdom idea changed in later times. Mingled with Greek idealism, the ideas of Philo, and the Persian doctrines of good and evil, the Messiah of the kingdom became the Redeemer of the church. Jewish believers waited for the Messiah to return soon and set up a world-wide kingdom, while gentile believers came to see Jesus as the Redeemer of the children of the church.
p170.s5.b1: The narrator does not simply disparage this change. Building on the Master’s life and teachings, and adding the Greek and Persian concepts of eternal life and the doctrine of Philo, Paul founded one of the most progressive human societies ever to exist on Urantia. But in the process Christ became the head of the church rather than the elder brother of each believer, and the concept of the kingdom in the individual heart was gravely weakened.

head: To whom
What the kingdom was
rows: The Jews
The Israelite community
The gentiles
The Christian church
Jesus
The sum of those individuals who have confessed faith in the fatherhood of God and dedicated themselves to doing his will — the spiritual brotherhood of man

p170.s5.b3: The church itself is not blamed. As a social outgrowth of the kingdom, its appearance was natural and even desirable. The trouble was that this social response almost completely displaced the spiritual kingdom that Jesus taught and lived. Membership in a church does not necessarily mean fellowship in the kingdom, for one is spiritual and the other mainly social.

p170.s5.b4.q: membership in the church does not necessarily mean fellowship in the kingdom; one is spiritual, the other mainly social.

p170.s5.b5.q: but you should comprehend that this church is only the larval stage of the thwarted spiritual kingdom

p170.s5.b6: The paper ends in hope. A greater John the Baptist will one day arise to call people back to Jesus’ lofty spiritual concept, and the church, the cocoon in which the kingdom now slumbers, will at last release it like a butterfly. The narrator adds that believers may differ in intellectual interpretation, but a lack of spiritual brotherhood among them is inexcusable.
p170.s6.b0: Paper 170 untangles a long confusion over a single word. For Jesus the kingdom was neither a territory nor an institution; it was the personal experience of knowing God as Father and seeking to do his will. That experience begins within, shows itself outwardly in loving service, and in time transforms societies and ages.

p170.s6.b2: In the next paper, Paper 171, “On the Way to Jerusalem,” Jesus leaves Pella and sets out on his final journey.
p171.lead: From Pella through Perea and Jericho toward Jerusalem: the warning to count the cost, Bartimeus and Zaccheus, the good done “as he passed by,” and the parable of the pounds.

p171.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p171.s0.h: Introduction — Seats on the Right Hand and the Left
p171.s0.b0: The day after the sermon on the kingdom of heaven, Jesus announced that he would leave for the Passover at Jerusalem, visiting the cities of southern Perea on the way. His followers took this to mean that he was at last going up to inaugurate the temporal kingdom of Jewish supremacy. Whatever he said about the nonmaterial character of the kingdom, the hope of a nationalistic government would not be erased.
p171.s0.b1: That Sunday afternoon Salome, the mother of James and John, came with her two sons and asked that in the kingdom one of them might sit on Jesus’ right hand and the other on his left. Jesus would make no promise in advance; instead he asked whether they could drink the cup he was about to drink. Without a moment’s thought the two answered that they could. When the other apostles heard of it, they were highly indignant.

p171.s0.b2.q: Whosoever would be great among you, let him first become your servant.

p171.s0.b3: That evening, thanks to Peter’s efforts, the two brothers apologized to the ten and were restored to their good graces. The narrator notes that they little realized that within a month their teacher would hang on a cross with a dying thief on one side and another transgressor on the other. This brief scene sharply exposes the gap between a heart that seeks honor and a Master who speaks of service.
p171.s1.h: I. The Departure from Pella — A Camp Breaks Up
p171.s1.b0: On the forenoon of Monday, March 13, Jesus and the twelve took final leave of the Pella encampment. About a thousand disciples followed, most of them convinced that he was now going to Jerusalem to lay claim to David’s throne. Two days later David Zebedee, on Andrew’s instructions, closed the visitors’ camp, where almost four thousand were staying, sold its equipment, and turned the money over to Judas Iscariot.
p171.s1.b1: David disliked the task but carried it out, and he was present in Jerusalem through the tragic last week. Later he went to Philadelphia, where he spent the rest of his life with Abner and Lazarus as financial overseer of the kingdom’s work there. Andrew’s order to end the messenger service was taken by everyone as a sign that the kingdom would soon be set up—a reminder that when expectations harden, the same event can be read in exactly the opposite way.
p171.s1.b2: Along with David’s later story, the narrator gives a glimpse of a parting of ways far in the future. After the destruction of Jerusalem, two centers carried Jesus’ teachings in different directions.

What it spread
Where it went

All the Western world
Philadelphia

p171.s2.h: II. On Counting the Cost — Sit Down and Reckon Before You Follow
p171.s2.b0: At the Bethany ford of the Jordan the disciples realized that Jesus was not going straight to Jerusalem, and they hesitated. Then Jesus climbed onto a huge stone and gave the discourse known as “⟦Q 171:2.1⟧Counting the Cost.⟦/Q⟧” From now on, he told them, following him would no longer mean listening to teaching and watching his works; it would mean bearing witness to the gospel in the face of bitter persecution and crushing disappointment.

p171.s2.b1.q: If you are not willing to pay the full price, you can hardly be my disciple.

head: Illustration
Lesson
rows: The man who builds a watchtower
If he does not first sit down and count the cost, he may lay the foundation and be unable to finish, and his neighbors will mock him
The king preparing for war
He first considers whether ten thousand can meet twenty thousand; if not, he asks for terms of peace while the enemy is still far off
Salt that has lost its savor
A disciple with worldly motives, seeking honor and glory, becomes useless

p171.s2.b3.q: If you have already conquered yourself within your own heart, you need have no fear of that outward victory

p171.s2.b4: After these words about half the crowd left him and went directly up to Jerusalem. Even those who stayed still believed that after a brief time of trial the kingdom would be established much as they had always hoped. The call to count the cost remains an honest question for believers today: before emotional enthusiasm, look first at your motives.
p171.s3.h: III–IV. The Perean Tour and Livias — Swords and Warnings
p171.s3.b0: For more than two weeks Jesus and the twelve went about the towns of southern Perea where the seventy were working. At Heshbon he met Abner, and this was the last time Abner saw him in the flesh. Jesus advised the messengers to go on with their work regardless of what was about to happen at Jerusalem. Day by day the number of followers dwindled, until fewer than two hundred remained.

p171.s3.b1.q: and I pray the Father to grant you wisdom that you may love and understand your brethren.

p171.s3.b2: The apostles knew the Sanhedrin had condemned him to death, yet they were less afraid than before. Having seen Lazarus raised, they had concluded that Jesus might, in an emergency, assert his divine power and put his enemies to shame. At Livias the two Simons secretly handed out more than a hundred swords. Jesus knew of it but never said so; early the next morning he gathered the apostles and once more told them plainly of his death and of his rising on the third day.

p171.s3.b3.q: I would now warn you not to put your trust in the uncertainties of the flesh nor in the frailties of man’s defense

p171.s3.b4: Most of the apostles and many of the inner disciples, believing him to be “⟦Q 171:3.5⟧the resurrection and the life,⟦/Q⟧” did not think it possible that he could die. When faith and expectation become entangled, even the clearest warning is bent to fit the hearer’s hopes. The fact that the Jews knew little or nothing of a suffering Messiah deepened the misunderstanding.
p171.s3.b5: The apostles could not take his words literally. The “third day” was a common expression for “soon,” so they took his “rising” to mean the rising of the kingdom. When friendly Pharisees warned that Herod sought to kill him, Jesus told them to tell that fox the course he would take, and he lamented over Jerusalem. The narrator adds that what sustained the Master in this trying period was the memory of the transfiguration.
p171.s4.h: V–VI. Two Men at Jericho — Bartimeus and Zaccheus
p171.s4.b0: Late on Thursday afternoon, March 30, near the gate of Jericho, Bartimeus, a beggar blind from his youth, heard that Jesus was passing by and began to cry out. The more people rebuked him, the louder he cried. Jesus stood still, had him brought over, asked what he wanted, and, seeing his faith, restored his sight.
p171.s4.b1: What stands out in the story is Jesus’ question. He did not guess at the man’s need and act first; he asked, “⟦Q 171:0.4⟧What do you want me to do for you?⟦/Q⟧” He had put the same question to Salome, but one asked for honor and the other for sight. Bartimeus, his sight restored, stayed near Jesus glorifying God until the Master left the next day.
p171.s4.b2: That same evening Zaccheus, the chief publican, being short of stature, climbed a sycamore tree to see Jesus. Jesus stopped beneath it and told him he would stay at his house that night. When a Pharisee grumbled that he was lodging with a sinner, Zaccheus stood on a stool and publicly promised to give half his goods to the poor and to restore fourfold whatever he had wrongfully exacted.

p171.s4.b3.q: Today has salvation come to this home, and you have become indeed a son of Abraham.

p171.s5.h: VII. “As Jesus Passed By” — Gracious Goodness
p171.s5.b0: Here the narrator pauses the story to portray Jesus’ character. He spread good cheer wherever he went and was full of grace and truth. His compassion was boundless, yet he seldom indulged in pity and never increased the self-pity of those who suffered. People felt not so much that they were confessing to him as that they were conferring with him.

p171.s5.b1.q: Goodness is universally attractive only when it is gracious. Goodness is effective only when it is attractive.

p171.s5.b2: He never sought to direct or manage people, yet he did not hesitate to be severe when the occasion demanded it. Great things happened not only because people had faith in him but also because he had so much faith in them. Most of the truly important things he said or did seemed to happen casually, “⟦Q 171:7.9⟧as he passed by.⟦/Q⟧”

p171.s5.b3.q: When he smiled on a man, that mortal experienced increased capacity for solving his manifold problems.

p171.s5.b4.q: And it behooves the Master’s followers in all ages to learn to minister as “they pass by”—to do unselfish good as they go about their daily duties.

p171.s6.h: VIII. Parable of the Pounds — Ability and Faithfulness
p171.s6.b0: Halfway up the road to Bethany, Jesus told the apostles the parable of the pounds. It drew on the actual history of Archelaus and his failed attempt to gain the rule of Judea. Just as that prince was rejected by his citizens, Jesus said, the Son of Man would be rejected in his spiritual rule. He made the twelve his special stewards and charged them to trade diligently with what had been entrusted to them.
p171.s6.b1: The servant who gained ten pounds was given ten cities; the one who gained five, five cities. The servant who feared his master and kept the pound wrapped in a napkin lost even that. When the apostles asked how this parable differed from the parable of the talents, Jesus only told them each to find the true meaning for themselves. In later years Nathaniel summed up the meaning of the two parables in four conclusions.

p171.s6.b3: After lunch Jesus pointed westward and said, “⟦Q 171:8.14⟧Come, my brethren, let us go on into Jerusalem, there to receive that which awaits us⟦/Q⟧.” So the Master’s last journey to Jerusalem in the likeness of mortal flesh was resumed.
p171.s7.b0: Paper 171 is a paper of the road to Jerusalem. The number of followers kept shrinking, and even those who stayed expected a kingdom of glory. Along that road Jesus taught service, warned his hearers to count the cost, and did not pass by the blind man or the publican at the roadside. The paper shows a life that, even while moving toward a great mission, cares for the one person in front of it.

p171.s7.b2: In the next paper, Paper 172, “Going into Jerusalem,” Jesus passes through Bethany and rides into Jerusalem on a donkey.
p172.lead: The feast at Bethany and Mary’s anointing, the entry into Jerusalem on a donkey, and the strikingly different responses that stirred in the twelve apostles that evening.

p172.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p172.s0.b0: Jesus and the apostles reached Bethany on Friday afternoon, March 31, A.D. 30. So many people came daily to talk with Lazarus about his resurrection that Jesus lodged with a neighboring believer named Simon. Many expected him to defy the Sanhedrin’s decree of death, enter Jerusalem, and proclaim himself king of the Jews. Lazarus, Martha, and Mary understood more fully that he was not that kind of king, and they dimly sensed that this might be his last visit.
p172.s0.b1: The chief priests chose not to seize him among his friends and decided to wait until he came into Jerusalem. Jesus knew all this, yet he remained majestically calm; his friends had never seen him more composed and congenial. The apostles, by contrast, watched over him through the night in pairs, many of them girded with swords. This contrast sets the tone for the whole paper.
p172.s0.b2: The paper covers three days, from the Friday arrival to Sunday night: the feast at Bethany, the Sunday-morning instructions, the entry on a donkey, a walk about the temple, and the varied reactions of the twelve. On the surface it is a triumphal procession, but the narrator also shows the currents of rejection and betrayal running beneath it.
p172.s1.h: I. Sabbath at Bethany — Mary’s Ointment
p172.s1.b0: On the evening after the Sabbath, the people of Bethany and Bethpage gave a public banquet at Simon’s home in honor of Jesus and Lazarus—a banquet held in open defiance of the Sanhedrin. Jesus had been playing with the children until he came to the table, and he talked with Simon about Joshua of old, whose namesake he was, and about the walls of Jericho.

p172.s1.b1.q: but I would cause the walls of prejudice, self-righteousness, and hate to crumble before this preaching of the Father’s love for all men.

p172.s1.b2: Near the close of the feast Mary opened a cruse of costly ointment, anointed the Master’s head, poured it on his feet, and wiped them with her hair. Some murmured at the waste, and Judas Iscariot went to Andrew saying the ointment should have been sold for the poor. Jesus laid his hand on Mary’s head and defended her: she had done a good thing in her heart.
p172.s1.b3: The ointment cost as much as a man’s earnings for a year—enough to feed five thousand—so the murmuring was understandable. But Jesus said that the poor are always with us to be served whenever we choose, while he was soon going to the Father. Love has its moment, and a heart that recognizes that moment should not be overruled by the logic of cost.

p172.s1.b4.q: Mary has reproved all of you in that by this act she evinces faith in what I have said about my death and ascension to my Father in heaven.

p172.s1.b5: Mary had believed his warnings about his death and had long saved to buy the ointment for his burial, and Lazarus and Martha heartily approved. The same scene worked on Judas very differently. He took the Master’s words as a personal reproof, and thoughts of revenge that had lingered in his subconscious now entered his open, conscious mind. That same day the chief priests concluded that Lazarus too must die.
p172.s2.h: II. Sunday Morning with the Apostles — Final Instructions
p172.s2.b0: On Sunday morning, in Simon’s garden, Jesus gave the twelve their final instructions before entering Jerusalem. They were to do no public work during this Passover, to stay near him, and to watch and pray. He knew that some carried hidden swords but said nothing of it. The apostles listened in silence as he reviewed their ministry from the day of their ordination.

p172.s2.b1.q: He instructed them to remain near him and to “watch and pray.”

p172.s2.b2: Jesus also warned Lazarus not to sacrifice his life to the vengefulness of the Sanhedrin, and a few days later, when officers came to arrest him, Lazarus fled to Philadelphia. The followers dimly sensed the coming crisis, but the Master’s unusual cheerfulness and good humor kept them from grasping how serious it was.
p172.s3.h: III. The Start for Jerusalem — The King of Peace on a Donkey
p172.s3.b0: Unlike Nazareth, Capernaum, and Jerusalem, Bethany had accepted him and believed in him. The narrator notes that he did not raise Lazarus so that the villagers might believe, but because they already believed. Until now Jesus had always suppressed public acclaim of himself as the Messiah, but this time he decided to let his disciples express their feelings freely.

p172.s3.b1.q: He did not raise Lazarus that the villagers might believe, but rather because they already believed.

p172.s3.b2.q: Jesus did not decide to make this public entrance into Jerusalem as a last bid for popular favor nor as a final grasp for power.

p172.s3.b3: Among the many conflicting Messianic prophecies, he took as his guide the words of Zechariah about a lowly king riding upon an ass. What he had failed to accomplish by plain teaching, he would attempt through a symbolic appeal. Peter and John brought the colt from Bethpage.

p172.s3.b5: As the procession climbed Olivet, the crowd spread their garments and branches and shouted hosannas. At the brow of the hill, where the city and temple came into view, Jesus halted the procession and wept, grieving that the city about to reject the Son of Peace did not know the time of its divine visitation. The thousands who came out from Jerusalem to meet him had been stirred up by David Zebedee and others; Jesus never premeditated anything dramatic.

p172.s3.b6.q: And all this shall befall you because you knew not the time of your divine visitation.

p172.s3.b7.q: It would be useless to stop them lest in their stead these stones by the roadside cry out.

p172.s3.b8: The Pharisees hurried ahead to the Sanhedrin and reported that the people had gone mad over him and that, unless he was stopped, all the world would go after him. The whole city was stirred, and people asked, “⟦Q 172:3.16⟧Who is this man?⟦/Q⟧” The multitude answered that he was the prophet of Galilee, Jesus of Nazareth. They hailed him as king, yet their answer stopped at “prophet.”
p172.s3.b9: The narrator states plainly that no deep significance should be attached to this enthusiasm. The welcome was joyous and sincere, but it reflected no deep-seated conviction. Later that same week, when they realized he would not set up the kingdom they expected, the same crowds were just as quick to reject him. The warning to distinguish acclaim from faith applies to religious communities in every age.
p172.s4.h: IV. Visiting about the Temple — The Widow’s Two Mites
p172.s4.b0: After the entry, Jesus and ten of the apostles strolled about the temple. The Sanhedrin, fearing the people, made no move against him. The apostles little understood it, but the public entry was the only human procedure that could have prevented his immediate arrest on entering the city. Through it Jesus gave the people of Jerusalem and the Passover pilgrims one last chance to receive the Son of Peace.
p172.s4.b1: Toward evening they sat by the treasury and watched people make their offerings. The rich put in much, and then a poor, scantily clad widow cast in two mites.

p172.s4.b2.q: but this poor woman, even though she is in want, gave all that she had, even her living.

p172.s4.b3: Mary’s costly ointment and the widow’s tiny coins stand at opposite ends in value, yet Jesus saw the same thing in both: each gave not according to the size of her possessions but with the whole of her heart.

p172.s5.h: V. The Apostles’ Attitude — Twelve Different Nights
p172.s5.b0: No one spoke on the way back to Bethany. The narrator says that no twelve human beings ever felt such diverse and inexplicable emotions, and he describes each apostle’s response in turn. The heart of the section is that the same event was received in entirely different ways according to each man’s temperament and expectations.

p172.s5.b2: John, Nathaniel, and Thomas each drew a little nearer to the meaning of the day—by way of symbol, of political reasoning, and of analysis. The twins simply enjoyed the day without analyzing it, and the memory carried them right up to the hour of the crucifixion. By contrast, Simon Zelotes and Peter, who had expected the most, were the most deeply disappointed. The passage quietly reminds us that the greater our expectations, the more a reality that does not match them can wound.
p172.s5.b3: For Judas the decisive moment was the ridicule of a Sadducee friend at the city gate. He had never shrunk from persecution, but he could not bear ridicule. To his long-nourished desire for revenge was now added the fear of being ashamed of his Master and his fellow apostles.

p172.s5.b4.q: At heart, this ordained ambassador of the kingdom was already a deserter

p172.s6.b0: Paper 172 depicts a day of acclaim, but at its center is the calm of a Master unmoved by applause. Choosing a donkey rather than a horse, he showed by a symbol the kingdom of peace, and in the middle of a joyful procession he wept for the city. Through the very different ways twelve men experienced the same day, the paper also shows how strongly expectation governs what we see.

p173.lead: Monday in Jerusalem: the cleansing of the temple, a counter-question to those who challenged his authority, and the parables of the two sons, the absent landlord, and the marriage feast.

p173.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p173.s0.h: Introduction — “What Will the Master Do Today?”
p173.s0.b0: Early on Monday morning Jesus and the apostles gathered at Simon’s home in Bethany and set out for Jerusalem. The apostles, not yet recovered from the previous day, were strangely silent. The Master’s sudden change of tactics, together with his instruction that they do no public teaching throughout the Passover week, had left them with a certain feeling of detachment.
p173.s0.b1: As they went down Mount Olivet, every apostle but Judas had one question uppermost in mind: What will the Master do today? Judas was absorbed by a different question: Should he go on with Jesus or withdraw, and if he withdrew, how should he break away? Walking the same road while holding such different questions, the group casts a tension over the whole paper.
p173.s0.b2: Arriving at the temple about nine o’clock, Jesus mounted a teaching platform in the large court where he so often taught, and the apostles stood a little way off to watch. The day unfolds in the cleansing of the temple, the dispute over authority, and three parables.
p173.s1.h: I. Cleansing the Temple — A House of Prayer Turned Marketplace
p173.s1.b0: The narrator first explains in detail how the temple courts had become a market. Sacrificial animals had to be without “blemish,” and many worshipers had suffered the humiliation of having their animals rejected by the temple inspectors. So the custom of buying animals at the temple took hold, and the larger part of the enormous profits went to the ruling high-priestly families.

head: Commerce in the temple
How it worked
rows: Sale of sacrificial animals
A high price in exchange for a guarantee against rejection — exorbitant overcharges at the feasts, once a week’s wages for a pair of doves
Money-changing
The half-shekel temple tax could be paid only in Jewish coin, so fees were charged for exchanging more than twenty sorts of money
Banking
All other kinds of banking transactions besides — the temple treasury at times held upwards of ten million dollars
The result
The common people languished in poverty while continuing to pay these unjust levies

p173.s1.b2: As Jesus was about to begin his address, three things converged: a heated argument over the alleged overcharging of a Jew from Alexandria, the bellowing of a drove of bullocks being driven across the court, and a simple-minded Galilean being ridiculed and jostled by supercilious Judeans. Together they produced one of those strange and periodic uprisings of indignant emotion in Jesus’ soul.
p173.s1.b3: Jesus stepped down from the platform, took a whip of cords from the lad driving the cattle, drove the animals out, and opened the gates of every pen. The pilgrims, electrified, began overturning the money-changers’ tables, and in less than five minutes all commerce had been swept from the temple. By the time the Roman guards arrived, all was quiet. The apostles, astonished, never lifted a hand.
p173.s1.b4: He was not alone in his indignation. The common people, especially pilgrims from foreign provinces, heartily resented this profiteering desecration of their national house of worship. For the rest of the day guards set by the people stood at every archway and would not let anyone carry even an empty vessel across the courts, and the temple was quiet and peaceful. The chief priests feared him all the more, yet because of the crowds they could not act.

p173.s1.b5.q: ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations, but you have made it a den of robbers.’

p173.s1.b6.q: Have you never read, ‘Out of the mouths of babes and sucklings has praise been perfected’?

p173.s1.b7: The narrator spells out the meaning of the episode. It reveals Jesus’ attitude toward the commercializing of religion and his detestation of every form of unfairness and profiteering at the expense of the poor and the unlearned. It also shows that he did not approve of refusing to use force to protect the majority when unjust minorities entrench themselves behind political, financial, or ecclesiastical power.

p173.s1.b8.q: This cleansing of the temple discloses the Master’s attitude toward commercializing the practices of religion as well as his detestation of all forms of unfairness and profiteering at the expense of the poor and the unlearned.

p173.s2.h: II. Challenging the Master’s Authority — Where Did John’s Baptism Come From?
p173.s2.b0: Both the triumphal entry and the cleansing of the temple had the effect of postponing his arrest. The leaders feared that the multitude might turn on them in fury, and that the Roman guards might be called in to quell a popular uprising. At its noon session the Sanhedrin agreed unanimously that Jesus must be speedily destroyed, but it could not settle on how, and so it sent out five groups to try to entangle him in his teaching.
p173.s2.b1: About two o’clock, just as Jesus had begun his discourse on “⟦Q 173:2.2⟧The Liberty of Sonship,⟦/Q⟧” a group of elders interrupted to ask by what authority he did these things. The narrator grants that the question itself was proper. Only the Sanhedrin could ordain a teacher, and public teaching without such authority was regarded as either ignorant presumption or open rebellion.
p173.s2.b2: Ordination had to take place before at least three persons previously ordained, and it conferred the title “rabbi” along with the right to act as a judge, “⟦Q 173:2.3⟧binding and loosing⟦/Q⟧” the matters brought before him. The prophets had always stirred up trouble precisely because they taught without such authority. The question, then, was more than a quibble: it was the moment when institutional authority and spiritual authority met face to face.
p173.s2.b3: Jesus answered with a question of his own: Was John’s baptism from heaven or from men? Finding either answer dangerous, they said they did not know, and Jesus in turn declined to tell them by what authority he acted. This was no evasion. Jesus never meant to rest his authority on John; it lay in himself and in his Father.

p173.s2.b4.q: Jesus’ authority was in himself and in his Father’s eternal supremacy.

head: Had they answered
The consequence they feared
rows: “From heaven”
He would ask why they had not believed John, and might add that he had received his authority from John
“From men”
The multitude, most of whom held John to be a prophet, might turn on them
“We do not know”
The religious leaders of Israel had to confess publicly that they could not judge John’s mission

p173.s2.b6.q: Jesus was never disposed to take unfair advantage of even his enemies.

p173.s2.b7: Even the common folk could tell the difference between the moral majesty of the Master and the designing hypocrisy of his enemies. Yet the cleansing of the temple had brought the Sadducees over to the side of the Pharisees in perfecting the plan to destroy Jesus, and the Sadducees now made up a majority of the Sanhedrin.
p173.s3.h: III. Parable of the Two Sons — Saying and Doing
p173.s3.b0: Before the silent Pharisees Jesus told the parable of the two sons. One said he would not go to work in the vineyard, but afterward repented and went; the other said, “⟦Q 173:3.1⟧Yes, my father, I will go⟦/Q⟧,” and did not go. The people answered with one accord that the first son had done his father’s will.

p173.s3.b1.q: you, who make great pretensions of serving the Father in heaven while you refuse to do the works of the Father.

p173.s3.b2.q: It was not you, the Pharisees and scribes, who believed John, but rather the publicans and sinners

p173.s3.b3: The narrator stresses that Jesus did not despise the Pharisees and Sadducees personally. What he sought to discredit was not the men but their systems of teaching and practice. What was taking place was the inevitable clash between a new and living religion of the spirit and the older religion of ceremony, tradition, and authority.
p173.s3.b4: All this while the twelve stood near the Master without taking any part. Each was reacting in his own way to the events of these closing days, yet each obeyed the instruction to refrain from public teaching. Standing silently at his side was, at times, a form of obedience.
p173.s4.h: IV. Parable of the Absent Landlord — The Rejected Stone Becomes the Cornerstone
p173.s4.b0: Jesus told the crowd another parable. A householder let out his vineyard to tenants and went away; when he sent servants to collect the fruits, the tenants beat and killed them, and at last they cast his son out of the vineyard and killed him too. The people answered that the lord would destroy those men and let the vineyard out to honest farmers.
p173.s4.b1: Some who perceived that the parable referred to the nation’s treatment of the prophets and its coming rejection of the gospel said in sorrow that they hoped such things would not go on. Turning to the leaders who were approaching, Jesus warned that if they kept rejecting the gospel, the kingdom of God would be given to a people who would bring forth the fruits of the spirit.

p173.s4.b2.q: whoso falls upon it, while he is thereby broken in pieces, shall be saved

p173.s4.b3: The leaders wanted to seize him but, fearing the crowd, withdrew; that night the Sadducees and Pharisees joined hands in a plan to entrap him the next day. The parable can be read less as a condemnation of a particular group than as a warning to any heart that withholds the fruits of what has been entrusted to it.
p173.s5.h: V. Parable of the Marriage Feast — The Garment Freely Provided
p173.s5.b0: After the leaders had withdrawn, Jesus spoke the parable of the wedding feast. The invited guests went their ways, one to the farm, another to the pottery, others to their merchandise, and some even mistreated and killed the messengers. So the king sent his servants into the highways and gathered everyone they found, good and bad, rich and poor, until the wedding chamber was filled.

p173.s5.b2.q: I will have none here except those who delight to accept my invitation, and who do me the honor to wear those guest garments so freely provided for all.

p173.s5.b3: When a believer asked how they could be ready and what sign he would give, Jesus pointed to his own body and said, “⟦Q 173:5.4⟧Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.⟦/Q⟧” Even the apostles did not understand, though after his resurrection they remembered his words. Climbing Olivet that night, the twelve sensed as never before that something tragic was about to happen.
p173.s5.b4: The apostles’ suspense reached its height. The morning’s cleansing of the temple had raised their hopes that the Master would at last assert his power, but the afternoon’s events all pointed to the certain rejection of his teaching by the authorities. They felt that something tremendous was about to happen without knowing what to expect, and even the Alpheus twins realized that events were moving swiftly toward their final culmination.
p173.s6.b0: Paper 173 records the day Jesus acted most decisively. He was indignant at the exploitation of the poor in the name of religion, and even when challenged about his authority he took no unfair advantage of his enemies. Through three parables he taught doing over saying, the duty to render the fruits of what has been entrusted to us, and the willingness to put on the grace freely given.
